newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries up sharply at midday after cost data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries up sharply at midday after cost data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were sharply higher at midday on Tuesday after getting a two-stage boost -- first from a more moderate-than-expected rise in the third-quarter employment cost index (ECI), and next from a drop in October consumer confidence.
The fixed-income market's first piece of good news on Tuesday was the 0.6 percent rise in the third-quarter ECI.
"The wage side was surprisingly moderate at 0.6 percent when most people were looking for 0.8 percent or 0.9 percent," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities.

"The tightness of the labor market is not being translated into higher wages, at least not yet," said Lieberman. "That makes it possible for the Fed to leave rates unchanged for the remainder of the year."

"There were two great pieces of information for the fixed-income market," said Elliott Platt, managing director, economist research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "Number one you had the employment cost index that indicated that compensation increased only 0.6 percent in the third quarter, a 2.4 percent annualized rate.
"That number becalmed inflation expectations and went a long way toward calming any lingering fears that the Fed might be tightening monetary policy anytime this year," said Platt.
The market doubled the gain it made after the ECI report when the Conference Board reported a drop in its October Consumer Confidence index.
"Consumer confidence, including buying plans for houses and automobiles, dropped very significantly," said Platt.
Another weak signal was a fall in the October APICS (American Production and Inventory Control Society) businesss outlook index, which slipped to 49.1 from 53.8 in September.
"The APICS survey came out weaker in most categories," said Lieberman, referring to significant declines in shipments, new orders and unfilled orders in the APICS index.

The APICS report said the declines, taken together, suggested "that the effect of higher interest rates on discretionary consumer spending and housing are now starting to take a toll on the manufacturing sector."
The market advanced against the backdrop of expectations for a weak third-quarter GDP (Gross Domestic Product) report on Wednesday.

"There's a lot of hope that the mix (of data in the GDP report) tomorrow will show a lot of inventories," said Lieberman. "Those people who are forecasting weak fourth quarters are counting on precisely that."
In early afternoon trade, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was trading to new highs on the day, up 1-17/32 to 100-13/32, yielding 6.72 percent, versus 6.84 percent just before the ECI ECI was released.
Bill rates were down with three-month rates off three basis points to 5.01 percent, six-month rates down five basis points to 5.10 percent and year-bill rates down eight basis points to 5.18 percent.
Two-year notes were up 8/32 to 100-5/32, yielding 5.79 percent. Five-year notes were up 20/32 to 100-15/32, yielding 6.14 percent.
The 6-1/2 percent ten-year note was up one point to 100-18/32 to 6.42 percent.
